channel.title: Automation Worker
channel.description: Field notes on automating real work: websites, workflows and the agents that run them.

item.title: The agentic web is arriving through the back office
item.description: Agents won't browse your website the way people do. They'll book, enrol and pay through whatever your site exposes as a clear, callable step. Most small organisations aren't ready, and the fix is smaller than it sounds.

item.title: Testing integrations against digital twins
item.description: You can't run a test suite against a live mailing list. A small, faithful stand-in for each vendor API lets the real workflow files run end to end on every change, without sending anything to anyone.

item.title: Running a coding agent unattended: what has to be true first
item.description: Letting an AI coding agent work on a server while nobody watches is less about the agent and more about the rails: typed specifications, scripts instead of clicks, hard stop rules and evidence in place of summaries.

item.title: One home per function
item.description: Most operational mess comes from the same fact living in two places. A simple rule — each function has one home, and everything else links to it — removes a surprising amount of coordination work.

item.title: Making this blog an open agentic website
item.description: This site now carries an assistant that answers from its own posts and can subscribe a reader, running entirely in the visitor's browser on their own AI key. Here's what that took on a static site, and what it deliberately doesn't do.

item.title: What MCP is, and why it matters to small teams
item.description: The Model Context Protocol gives AI assistants one standard way to reach tools and data. It lowers the cost of connecting things, but a connector you click through every time is still not automation.

item.title: n8n or Windmill? Decide who owns the process first
item.description: Workflow tools overlap, so the useful question isn't which one is better. It's which tool owns the order of the steps, and which one only talks to vendors. Keeping those apart is what lets you swap a vendor without touching the process.

item.title: Wiring the newsletter with Brevo: adopt before you build
item.description: Subscriber lists, consent and unsubscribe are solved problems with legal weight. This blog hands all three to Brevo and keeps its own code to the part that's actually specific: one email per published post.

item.title: Why this blog is a static Astro site
item.description: A newsletter-first blog needs fast pages, typed content and nothing on a server to patch. Astro gives that without giving up components, and it compares well with Hugo for a site that will grow an assistant.
